# Worksheet: from equations to an epidemic curve

**~45 minutes**

In the last session you wrote the SIR kernel but never ran it. Here you hand it
to a solver and get an epidemic curve out, then check that curve against two
things the theory predicts in advance: that the population is conserved, and
that the infectious peak arrives exactly when the susceptible fraction falls
through $1/R_0$. Part B defines $R_0$.

Nothing here changes the model. The ordinary differential equations session is
where the model starts responding to interventions; today is about getting a
trustworthy curve and knowing why you trust it.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there; not
reaching it is completely fine. Worked solutions are posted at the end of each
day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

**Prefer sliders to typing?** The
[Pluto notebook](../../notebooks/chapters/01-foundations.jl) for this chapter
lets you drag $\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$ and watch $R_0$ and the curve respond.
Some people find the intuition easier there first. Either order is fine.

**Coming from R?**

| R | Julia | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `f <- function(x) x^2` | `f(x) = x^2` | or `function f(x) ... end` |
| `x <- c(1, 2, 3)` | `x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]` | `1.0` and `1` are different types |
| `list(a = 1, b = 2)` | `(a = 1, b = 2)` | a named tuple; read fields with `p.a` |
| `m[2, ]` | `m[2, :]` | the `:` means "all of this dimension" |

Indexing starts at 1, as in R. A `!` at the end of a name (`sir_ode!`) means the
function modifies its argument rather than returning a copy.

The [Julia essentials chapter](../../prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd)
has the full table.

---

## Setup

This is your kernel from the last session, given back so that nobody is held up
retyping work they have already done. Note the two reading
conventions it uses, because everything below follows them: the **state** `u` is
positional (`S, I, R = u`), the **parameters** `p` are read by field (`p.β`).

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-setup
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using NonlinearSolve
using CairoMakie

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
    du[3] = p.γ * I
    return nothing
end

u0    = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]                          # S(0), I(0), R(0)
p     = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
tspan = (0.0, 80.0)

println("kernel ready; R₀ = ", p.β * p.c / p.γ)
```

---

## Part A — solve it, then read the answer (~15 min)

Solving takes two steps. An `ODEProblem` bundles *what the model is*: the
kernel, where it starts, how long to run, and the parameters. `solve` then says
*how to integrate it*: here `Tsit5()`, a general-purpose method that is a good
default for models like this one.

Read the next cell before running it. The four-argument order is worth
recognising, because you will write it yourself repeatedly from here on:

```julia
ODEProblem(kernel, initial_state, timespan, parameters)
```

The kernel goes in by *name*, with no brackets after it: you are handing the
solver the function itself, not calling it. `saveat = 0.5` asks the solver to
store the solution every half day; it does not change how the solver steps
internally, only what it keeps for you.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-a1
prob = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p)
sol  = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5)

check("the solver ran", sol.retcode == ReturnCode.Success)
check("it stored one state every half day", length(sol.t) == 161)

sol.u[end]       # the whole state vector at day 80
```

Three numbers came back: $S$, $I$ and $R$ at day 80. Almost everyone has been
infected and recovered, and the epidemic is over.

Now read the result. A solution can be read three ways, and each answers a
different question:

| Idiom | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| `sol.t` | the times that were stored |
| `sol.u` | a vector of **whole state vectors**, one per stored time |
| `sol[i, :]` | **compartment `i`** across every stored time |

`sol.u[end]` above used the second. For plotting a single compartment you want
the third.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-a2
t = sol.t
S = sol[1, :]
I = Float64[]     # TODO: replace this — the infectious compartment, all stored times
R = sol[3, :]

check("one value of I per stored time", length(I) == length(t))
check("the epidemic took off", !isempty(I) && maximum(I) > u0[2])
check("nobody is created or destroyed",
      all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), p.N; atol = 1e-6), sol.u))

isempty(I) || println("peak infectious: ", round(maximum(I), digits = 1),
                      " on day ", round(t[argmax(I)], digits = 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

```julia
I = sol[2, :]
```

`I` is the second compartment, so the first index is `2`; the `:` means "every
stored time". Compare the `S` line directly above it.

The conservation check uses `sol.u` rather than `sol[i, :]` because it needs
each *whole* state at once: it adds $S+I+R$ at each time and compares with $N$.
That is the distinction between the second and third rows of the table.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch01-sir
#| fig-cap: "Baseline SIR epidemic: susceptible, infectious and recovered over 80 days."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "number of individuals")
lines!(ax, t, S; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, label = "S")
isempty(I) || lines!(ax, t, I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "I")
lines!(ax, t, R; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 3, label = "R")
axislegend(ax; position = :rc)
fig
```

### A1. Interpret

- `sol.u` is a vector whose elements are themselves vectors, while `sol[2, :]`
  is a plain vector of numbers. Which shape did the figure need, and why?
- The conservation check passed to within $10^{-6}$ rather than exactly. Where
  does that last bit of error come from?
- Nothing in the kernel says the population is fixed; we never wrote $S+I+R=N$
  anywhere. So why does it hold?

> *Your answer here.*

---

## Part B — the threshold, and when nothing happens (~15 min)

The basic reproduction number is the average number of secondary infections one
infectious person produces in a fully susceptible population:

$$
R_0 = \frac{\beta c}{\gamma}.
$$

The epidemic grows only while $S/N > 1/R_0$. That makes a sharp, checkable
prediction: the infectious curve turns over at the *exact moment* the
susceptible fraction crosses $1/R_0$ — not near it, at it.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-b1
R₀ = 0.0     # TODO: replace 0.0 — compute R₀ from the fields of p

peak_index = isempty(I) ? 1 : argmax(I)
S_over_N_at_peak = S[peak_index] / p.N

check("R₀ is 2 for the baseline", isapprox(R₀, 2.0; atol = 1e-9))
check("the peak sits on the threshold",
      R₀ > 0 && isapprox(S_over_N_at_peak, 1 / R₀; atol = 0.01))

(R₀ = R₀, threshold = R₀ > 0 ? 1 / R₀ : NaN, S_over_N_at_peak = S_over_N_at_peak)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B, R₀

```julia
R₀ = p.β * p.c / p.γ
```

To type `R₀`: `R\_0`↹. Plain `R0` works just as well if you prefer it; the
subscript is cosmetic.

If the threshold check fails but `R₀` is right, look at `peak_index`: `argmax`
returns the *position* of the largest value, which is what you want here, not
the value itself.
:::

Now vary the contact rate. Everything else stays at baseline, so $R_0$ scales
with $c$ and there is some contact rate below which the epidemic never takes
off.

`p` is a named tuple, which cannot be modified in place. `merge` builds a new
one with some fields replaced and the rest carried over:

```julia
merge(p, (c = 4.0,))     # same parameters, but with contact rate 4
```

(The trailing comma is required: it is what makes `(c = 4.0,)` a one-field
named tuple rather than a bracketed expression.)

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-b2
contact_rates = [4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0]
results = map(contact_rates) do c_val
    p_c = p     # TODO: replace p — the baseline parameters with contact rate c_val
    s   = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p_c), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5)
    (c = c_val,
     R₀ = round(p_c.β * p_c.c / p_c.γ; digits = 2),
     peak_I = round(maximum(s[2, :]); digits = 1),
     infected_by_80 = round(s[3, end] / p.N; digits = 3))
end

check("each run used its own contact rate",
      length(unique(r.R₀ for r in results)) == 4)
check("c = 4 gives R₀ below 1", results[1].R₀ < 1)
check("no epidemic at c = 4", results[1].peak_I <= u0[2])
check("the day-80 total climbs with contact rate",
      let a = [r.infected_by_80 for r in results]; issorted(a) && allunique(a) end)

results
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B, the sweep

```julia
p_c = merge(p, (c = c_val,))
```

The loop variable is called `c_val` rather than `c` on purpose: `p.c` is already
the contact rate, and shadowing it inside the loop makes the code much harder to
read.

If every row comes out with the same `R₀`, `p_c` is still the unmodified `p`:
`merge` returns a new tuple rather than changing the old one, so its result has
to be assigned.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch01-threshold
#| fig-cap: "Infectious curves across contact rates. Below c = 5 the reproduction number falls under 1 and the initial infections fade without an epidemic."
fig2 = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax2  = Axis(fig2[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
            title = "Contact rate and the epidemic threshold")
for c_val in contact_rates
    s = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, merge(p, (c = c_val,))), Tsit5();
              saveat = 0.5)
    lines!(ax2, s.t, s[2, :]; linewidth = 3, label = "c = $(Int(c_val))")
end
axislegend(ax2; position = :rt)
fig2
```

### B1. Interpret

- At $c = 4$ the number of infectious people falls from day zero. Some people
  are still infected along the way, so in what sense is this "no epidemic"?
- The threshold condition is about $S/N$, not about how many people are
  infectious. Two outbreaks with very different $I$ can be on opposite sides of
  it. What does that say about using current case counts to judge whether an
  epidemic is under control?
- The same step in contact rate, $\Delta c = 2$, adds about 28 points to
  `infected_by_80` between $c = 4$ and $c = 6$ but only about 15 between
  $c = 8$ and $c = 10$, while the *peak* nearly doubles across that upper
  range. Where on
  the $R_0$ scale does an intervention buy the most, and does your answer change
  if what you care about is the peak rather than the total?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — the final size, without simulating (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

You already know how many had been infected by day 80 at each contact rate: you
simulated it and read the number off. The total ever infected, however far into
the future you look, can be obtained directly from $R_0$ without running the
model at all. The surviving susceptible fraction
$s_\infty = S(\infty)/N$ satisfies

$$
s_\infty = s_0 \exp\bigl(-R_0 (1 - s_\infty)\bigr),
\qquad s_0 = \frac{S(0)}{N},
$$

which cannot be rearranged for $s_\infty$ in elementary functions: it appears on
both sides and inside the exponential. (There is a closed form in terms of the
Lambert $W$ function, which is not much help unless you already have $W$.) In
practice it is found numerically, by searching for the value that makes the two
sides equal.

That is a *root-finding* problem, and it uses the same `solve` you have been
calling all session. Only the problem type changes: `NonlinearProblem` instead
of `ODEProblem`, and the function you supply returns the **residual**
(left-hand side minus right-hand side), which the solver drives to zero.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-c1
s₀ = u0[1] / p.N

# The residual takes the unknown and the parameters, mirroring f(du, u, p, t).
residual(s, R0) = s - s₀ * exp(-R0 * (1 - s))
# TODO: replace 0.0 with an initial guess for s∞ — anything up to about 0.6 will do
fs_prob = NonlinearProblem(residual, 0.0, R₀)

s_inf = solve(fs_prob, NewtonRaphson()).u
attack_rate = 1 - s_inf

check("s∞ is a fraction", 0 < s_inf < 1)
check("it really is a root", isapprox(residual(s_inf, R₀), 0.0; atol = 1e-8))

# Compare against simulation: run far past the end of the epidemic.
sol_long = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, (0.0, 400.0), p), Tsit5();
                 reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10, save_everystep = false)
simulated = sol_long.u[end][1] / p.N

check("analytic and simulated agree", isapprox(s_inf, simulated; atol = 1e-3))

(s_infinity = round(s_inf; digits = 4),
 simulated = round(simulated; digits = 4),
 attack_rate = round(attack_rate; digits = 4))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

```julia
fs_prob = NonlinearProblem(residual, 0.2, R₀)
```

Any guess below about 0.6 lands on the root you want. The residual turns over at
$s = 1 - \ln(s_0 R_0)/R_0 \approx 0.66$, and from above that point Newton's method
converges instead to a second root at $s_\infty \approx 1.010$. That is a genuine
solution of the equation, but it describes a negative attack rate, so it is not
an epidemic.

Try `0.9` as well as `0.2` and watch the "s∞ is a fraction" check fail. A
root-finder returns *a* root; nothing in the mathematics says which one you
meant.
:::

### C1. Interpret

- Roughly 80% of the population is infected over the epidemic, yet the model
  stops with 20% still susceptible. Transmission did not run out of people.
  What did it run out of?
- The analytic answer needed only $R_0$ and $s_0$. It never asked about
  $\beta$ and $c$ separately, or about $\gamma$ on its own. What does the
  simulated curve tell you that the final-size relation cannot?

> *Your answer here.*
